topic: How do GEO satellite propagation delays influence link budget margins for latency-sensitive applications?
consensus_response: GEO satellite propagation delays significantly impact link budget margins for latency-sensitive applications, introducing a fixed latency of several hundred milliseconds that degrades Quality of Service (QoS) and causes performance overhead. To mitigate this impact, increasing transmission power, buffering, congestion control, and using LEO/MEO satellites can help. Operating satellite backhaul networks at layer 2 can also reduce latency, although this requires balancing trade-offs between layer 2 and layer 3 operations in terms of scalability and cost. Latency-aware routing protocols, such as latency-sensitive routing (LSR), can be optimized to ensure real-time data flows through the lowest-latency paths, minimizing computational overhead and network complexity. However, these strategies have limitations and trade-offs, requiring careful consideration of the specific requirements and constraints of each application and network architecture.
reference_context: GEO satellites operate at a height of approximately 36,000 km, introducing a fixed latency of several hundred milliseconds. The high capacity of satellite links can be beneficial for exchanging large amounts of data, but the additional delay has a negative impact on QoS and applications that are not tolerant against high latencies, such as real-time or interactive applications. Protocol state machines and specific functionalities may need to be adopted to cope with the higher latency, and the standard congestion control mechanisms of TCP rely on the round-trip time (RTT) and thus suffer significantly from the high latency on satellite links.
